papers.title: Oxidative stress and lipidocentric mechanism of hyperglycemic glycolaldehyde damage to skeletal muscle cells
papers.abstract: Currently, diabetes-induced skeletal muscle complications affect over half of diabetic patients yet the pathway by which this hyperglycemic damage occurs has yet to be fully elucidated. As such, the goal of this study is to investigate the hypothesis: Glucose-derived glycolaldehydes, glyoxal and methylglyoxal, formed in hyperglycemia cause damage to the skeletal muscle myoblasts through oxidative stress and formation of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids upon activation of phospholipase A2 (PLA2) and cyclooxygenase (COX). To test this hypothesis skeletal muscle myoblasts, C2C12s, were exposed to various concentrations of glyoxal and methylglyoxal then tested for metabolic activity, reactive oxygen species production, redox status, ATP production, membrane integrity, cellular proliferation, enzyme activity, and loss of mitochondrial lipids. Doses of the agonist at 1 mM and 2 mM showed significant changes in all tested areas and were significantly attenuated by NAC, Ibuprofen, AACOCF3 and metformin. For the first time, these results suggest a plausible pathway by which diabetes-induced skeletal muscle deterioration occurs and identifies possible therapeutic endpoints.

papers.title: GnotoBag: A versatile peat-based gnotobiotic system for plant microbiome research beyond model species
papers.abstract: Plants and their microbial communities form a symbiotic system, where microbial communities play a key role in plant growth, development and stress resilience. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying plant-microbiota interactions remain poorly understood. A practical challenge is maintaining axenic conditions during prolonged plant growth while providing adequate space, ventilation, water, and nutrients. To advance research on plant-microbiome interactions, we developed the "GnotoBag" system, a bag-based extension of a previously established peat-based gnotobiotic plant growth platform. Key improvements of this GnotoBag system include enhanced ventilation and an integrated nutrient and water delivery system that sustains plant growth. These modifications support prolonged cultivation beyond the previously described 6.5-week workflow, enabling studies of microbiome effects on Arabidopsis thaliana growth and development under controlled microbial conditions, including the transition from vegetative to reproductive growth. Additionally, the expanded headspace of the GnotoBag provides sufficient space for cultivating larger plants, including rice and tomato, for at least four weeks. The increased headspace and the ability to add nutrients and water support research on larger crop plants, laying a foundation for future studies of microbiome functions in agricultural production.

papers.title: Ecological Feedback Dimensionality and Trade-Off Shape Govern Cancer Phenotypic Diversification
papers.abstract: Cancer cells face a variety of trade-offs in their microenvironment, from competition vs. colonization to immune evasion vs. rapid proliferation. Whether such trade-offs drive cancer cell populations to a single optimal phenotype or to a stable coexistence of phenotypes depends on the trade-off's shape and the number of independent ecological feedbacks that cells impose on each other and on their environment. We introduce trade-off and invasion plots (TIPs), a geometric tool from adaptive dynamics that determines the evolutionary outcome from the curvature of a trade-off relative to a pair of invasion boundaries, to cancer and ground our analysis in simple consumer-resource metabolic models. We show that the dimension of the ecological feedback determines whether diversification can occur: a one-dimensional feedback leads to monomorphism, whereas a two-dimensional feedback can promote evolutionary branching to a stable dimorphism. Furthermore, we show that the curvature of the allocation trade-off governs whether a single metabolic generalist (attractor), a stable dimorphism of specialists (evolutionary branching), or a single specialist (repellor) occurs. Both results are cancer-specific instances of long-established principles in theoretical ecology, namely the bound that the dimension of the feedback environment places on coexistence, and the fitness-set geometry relating trade-off curvature to specialization. Our contribution therefore primarily lies in bringing this mature eco-evolutionary machinery to bear on intratumoral heterogeneity.

papers.title: O2 exchange profiling reveals physiological diversity among taxonomically characterized green microalgal strains
papers.abstract: Taxonomic identification provides essential information about microalgae, but a shared species assignment does not necessarily imply similar physiological behavior. This study combined microscopy, ribosomal DNA sequencing, and O2 exchange measurements to characterize 20 green microalgal strains, comprising 18 environment-derived and two previously identified model strains. Net O2 evolution and post illumination consumption were measured across 17 increasing irradiances in three independently grown cultures per strain. Maximum differences between pair means for net O2 evolution were 18.12, 7.82, and 10.50 micromol O2 L/min for the Chlorella sorokiniana, Desmodesmus abundans, and Tetradesmus/Acutodesmus obliquus pairs at 100, 50, and 300 micromol photons m/s, respectively; all three cultures of one strain exceeded all three of the other at those irradiances. Within-pair ITS sequences differed by at most one nucleotide over the shared regions. Separately normalized profiles formed five exploratory groups, but group membership was sensitive to culture resampling, the number of principal components, and rate-extraction windows. Physiological distances showed no clear association with 18S patristic distances or assigned genus. Interpretation is limited by provisional species assignments, three cultures per strain, and a single ascending irradiance sequence that confounds light intensity with elapsed time and unmeasured carbon availability. O2 exchange profiling therefore provides complementary information about individual strains under a common experimental protocol, without establishing stable physiological classes or steady-state capacities.

papers.title: Beyond IgG: Oral Secretory IgA as a new efficient modality for cancer immunotherapy
papers.abstract: Monoclonal antibody therapies have revolutionized cancer treatment but are almost exclusively based on intravenously administered IgG antibodies. Here, we developed and evaluated the first orally delivered anti-CEACAM5 secretory IgA (SIgA) for colorectal cancer. The pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, antitumor efficacy and immune effects of oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) were evaluated in an orthotopic metastatic human colorectal cancer model. Its therapeutic activity was compared with cetuximab, as monotherapy and in combination with irinotecan- or FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy along with that of an anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 sharing the same antigen-binding domain. Tumor-associated FcRI (CD89)-expressing myeloid populations were characterized at primary and metastatic sites. ABC-101 activity was evaluated on a second human cancer cell line, in vivo in an orthotopic human gastric cancer model. Oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) exhibited a unique pharmacokinetic profile, selectively accumulating in CEACAM5-positive primary tumors and metastases while maintaining minimal systemic exposure. Compared with the anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 and cetuximab, oral SIgA achieved superior inhibition of primary tumor growth and metastatic dissemination. It also enhanced the efficacy of irinotecan- and FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy, outperforming the FOLFIRI/cetuximab standard-of-care comparator. Mechanistically, ABC-101 remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting the recruitment of FcRI (CD89)-expressing neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells at both primary and metastatic sites, consistent with enhanced innate antitumor activity. Oral ABC-101 shows targeted activity against CEAhigh MKN-45 cells, reducing markers of cell proliferation and migration. These findings establish therapeutic SIgA as a first-in-class oral antibody immunotherapy combining selective tumor targeting, innate immune activation, and enhanced chemotherapy efficacy. More broadly, this work establishes mucosal immunity as a promising therapeutic frontier, demonstrating that orally delivered antibodies can enable systemic control of metastatic digestive cancers.

papers.title: Functional divergence of D-, A-, and B-type cyclins in the moss Physcomitrium patens
papers.abstract: Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are central cell-cycle regulators that have undergone diversification in land plants; however, the functional implications of this divergence remain incompletely understood, particularly in non-vascular lineages. Here, we systematically dissected the roles of the three principal cyclin classes--D, A, and B--in the model moss Physcomitrium patens. We show that CYCD2 exhibits constitutive expression throughout the cell cycle, CYCA2 is degraded during mitosis and transcriptionally activated post-mitotically, whereas CYCB1 is M-phase-specific and rapidly depleted at anaphase. Overexpression and loss-of-function analyses revealed functional divergence among these classes: cyclin D primarily governs cell cycle entry and vegetative growth; cyclin B regulates mitotic progression with its overexpression causing division failure and arresting gametophore development; cyclin A regulates S-to-G2/M transition and exhibits overlapping functions with both D- and B-type cyclins, contributing to vegetative growth, mitotic fidelity, and gametophore development. Yeast two-hybrid assays showed that CYCB2 associates broadly with both CDKAs and CDKBs, CYCA2 preferentially interacts with CDKAs, and CYCD1 binds CDKAs along with a subset of CDKBs. Collectively, our results reveal both overlapping and class-specific contributions of D-, A-, and B-type cyclins to cell-cycle progression and development in P. patens, and suggest that complex tissues (gametophores) are particularly vulnerable to mitotic cyclin dysfunction. These findings provide a foundation for understanding how cyclin diversification underpins developmental plasticity across different contexts in non-vascular land plants.

papers.title: The Tomato Isochorismate Synthase Coordinates both Salicylic Acid-Mediated Immunity and Phylloquinone-Dependent Chloroplast Function
papers.abstract: Isochorismate synthase (ICS) provides isochorismate for salicylic acid (SA) and phylloquinone biosynthesis, yet how these functions are integrated in crop species remains poorly understood. We investigated the biological role of the single ICS gene in tomato. CRISPR/Cas9-generated ics mutants were analysed using pathogen assays, targeted and untargeted metabolomics, transcriptomics, chloroplast imaging, photosynthetic measurements and polysome profiling. Loss of ICS strongly reduced pathogen-induced SA accumulation and compromised Pto-mediated resistance to Pseudomonas syringae. Mutants also displayed severe growth defects, near-complete phylloquinone depletion, impaired photosynthetic performance and profound chloroplast ultrastructural alterations. Supplementation with the phylloquinone precursor 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoic acid partially restored photosynthetic performance. ICS disruption further caused extensive metabolic and transcriptional reprogramming and reduced polysome loading. These results reveal that the single tomato ICS gene contributes to two major outputs of isochorismate metabolism: pathogen-associated SA accumulation and phylloquinone-dependent chloroplast function. Together with emerging evidence for phenylalanine-derived SA biosynthesis in tomato, our findings indicate that SA biosynthetic routes are context-dependent and highlight substantial functional diversification of ICS across plant species.

papers.title: Puya: A new example of adaptive radiation in the Northern Andes
papers.abstract: Most documented examples of plant adaptive radiations occur on oceanic islands, but high-elevation mountain systems offer similar ecological opportunities. Here, we investigate the genus Puya (Bromeliaceae), a rapidly diversifying Andean lineage associated with high-elevation ecosystems, to assess how ecological opportunity and biotic interactions shape diversification and morphological evolution in fragmented mountain landscapes. Using a phylogenomic dataset for the Septentrional Clade of Puya, a clade largely restricted to the paramo habitat, we performed biogeographic reconstructions and trait evolution analyses using parametric models. We identified a temporal increase in diversification rates consistent with the onset of paramo expansion, together with a clade-specific increase in lineages associated with this ecosystem. Likewise, we found that character displacement and competitive exclusion drove phenotypic divergence and identified signatures of pulsed evolution. We propose the Septentrional Clade of Puya as a new example of adaptive radiation in continental sky-island systems and demonstrate that ecological opportunity and biotic interactions jointly shaped its evolutionary history. Our findings provide new insights into how ecological pressures shape macroevolutionary patterns in highly diverse plant clades and show that mountain radiations can generate morphological diversity through processes comparable to those documented in classic examples of adaptive radiations in oceanic islands.

papers.title: Evolutionary dynamics of Gag-restricted prion-like domains in LTR retroelements
papers.abstract: Background: Prions are proteins that can self-template, giving rise to non-Mendelian inheritance. They are functionally diverse and have been found in all domains of life and even beyond cellular life within viruses, a distribution that suggests an ancient evolutionary origin. Testing that origin has been difficult, as prions are identified by composition, such as an enrichment of Q/N residues, and are carried by rapidly changing disordered domains that are difficult to study phylogenetically. Long terminal repeat (LTR) retroelements, mobile genetic elements that replicate through an RNA intermediate and include both retrotransposons and retroviruses, are well suited to investigate prion evolution. Prion-like domains (PrLDs) occur in their Gag proteins, while their conserved Pol proteins allow phylogenetic reconstruction independent of the domains themselves. Results: Here, we screened 2,636 proteins from mobile genetic elements in the GyDB and identified 26 PrLDs. All 26 occurred in Gag, the only one of 74 protein categories to carry them, and this association remained significant when proteins were matched for intrinsic disorder, indicating that PrLDs are not a by-product of the high disorder of Gag. Gag PrLDs were found mainly in the C-terminal half of the protein. Their composition matched that of validated yeast and archaeal prion domains in glutamine and asparagine enrichment and charge depletion, with elevated aromatic content in common with the archaeal domains and an unusually high proline content. Across a phylogeny of 258 elements built from Pol, PrLD presence was clustered rather than randomly distributed, the root was reconstructed as PrLD-positive, and losses outpaced gains by roughly eighteenfold. Conclusions: Our findings establish PrLDs as a general feature of Gag across LTR retroelements, reveal a proline-rich composition that sets them apart from characterised prion domains, and trace their presence to the ancestor of these elements. Their retention across three superfamilies despite frequent loss points to maintenance rather than repeated acquisition. By mapping a compositionally defined domain onto a phylogeny built from conserved proteins, this work allows the gain and loss of prion-like sequence to be reconstructed and provides 26 candidates for experimental testing.

papers.title: Paraburkholderia endosymbionts with streamlined genomes are disadvantaged during interspecific competition
papers.abstract: Trait loss and genome size reduction are classic evolutionary signatures of obligate bacterial endosymbiosis. However, many bacteria are facultative endosymbionts and so experience a trade-off between adaptation to living within their hosts and apart from them. A central tension in this transition is whether traits required for independent life, including adaptations for interspecific competition, are maintained or lost. We compared three facultatively endosymbiotic Paraburkholderia species associated with the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum to test whether host adaptation is associated with reduced competitive ability. Two species, P. bonniea and P. hayleyella, display relatively small, streamlined genomes, while the other, P. agricolaris, has an unreduced genome compared to free-living congeners. We competed these species and three non-amoeba-associated Paraburkholderia against six ecologically relevant competitor bacteria, using fluorescent markers to track strain-specific fitness in co-culture. The reduced-genome species were never more competitive than P. agricolaris and, unlike P. agricolaris, never outcompeted their competitors. This deficit was reflected in a reduced ability to grow quickly to high levels in co-culture. Follow-up assays revealed that cell-free supernatant from the co-culture of P. agricolaris and a Pseudomonas isolate inhibited subsequent growth of the Pseudomonas, whereas supernatant from the co-culture of P. hayleyella and Pseudomonas did not. Reduced genome size in these facultative endosymbionts is associated with weaker competitive performance without eliminating independent proliferation under laboratory conditions. This competitive erosion may lead to ecological host dependence, where symbionts remain physiologically capable of living independently but become increasingly unable to persist outside the host in competitive microbial communities.

papers.title: High dietary sucrose reveals distinct roles for the BBSome subunits BBS1 and BBS9 in Drosophila development
papers.abstract: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes occur in Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and BBSome proteins regulate insulin receptor abundance at the cell surface in mammals. We asked how loss of two structurally related BBSome subunits, BBS1 and BBS9, affects development on a high-sucrose diet in Drosophila melanogaster. Sequence comparisons identified the seven-bladed beta-propeller and gamme-adaptin ear domains of human BBS1 and BBS9 in their respective fly orthologues. High sucrose (1 M) delayed pupariation in both single mutants, with the longest delay in flies lacking both subunits. The double mutant already showed a delay on standard sucrose (0.15 M). On high sucrose, its first pupae were recorded at 216 h after egg laying, whereas the last control and single-mutant pupae had formed by 168 h. Loss of BBS1 also reduced pupal volume and adult wing area on high sucrose. Both measurements remained close to control values in BBS9 mutants. These findings suggest overlapping contributions of BBS1 and BBS9 to developmental timing and a greater requirement for BBS1 to sustain growth under high dietary sucrose.

papers.title: Development of a Novel Multitarget Directed Ligand (MTDL), LCI132 for the Polypharmaceutical Treatment of High-Risk MYCN Amplified Neuroblastoma
papers.abstract: MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma (MNA-NB) is associated with poor prognosis due to the development of resistance to current aggressive therapy and to the subsequent limited response to single agent targeted therapeutics in the relapse setting. Herein, we describe the in silico design and development of the first-in-class nanomolar potent, selective, multitarget directed ligand (MTDL) against PI3K, BRD4, CDK4/6/9 and Aurora kinases A/B, LCI132, for the polypharmaceutical treatment of MNA-NB. LCI132 demonstrates a favorable safety and pharmacokinetics profile, suppresses viability, induces apoptosis in MNA-NB and inhibits in vivo tumor growth with no toxicity. Mechanistically our data show that LCI132 orthogonally inhibits MYCN transcription and induces proteasome mediated MYCN degradation. We and others recently observed an augmented cytostatic effect of combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with retinoic acid in MNA-NB models and the associated disruption of core regulatory circuits. Importantly, this was not associated with the induction of apoptosis. The combined treatment of MNA-NB cells with retinoic acid and LCI132 synergistically inhibited cellular proliferation and induced apoptosis in MNA-NB cell lines and ex vivo patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Combination of LCI132 and ATRA treatment effectively reduces levels of MYCN and alters the expression of CRC transcription factors. Collectively, our study provides mechanistic insights and a rationale for the combined use of ATRA and a MTDL, LCI132 as a novel polypharmaceutical therapeutic strategy for the treatment of MNA-NB NB.

papers.title: The PD-L1 metabolic interactome in glioma is bounded by IDH1 genotype
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has failed in glioblastoma, and part of the reason may lie in the tumour cell itself: if the checkpoint and the metabolism that sustains the cell hold each other up, then lowering one arm hands the tumour the other, and a single agent cannot win. We tested that possibility in GL261 glioma cells of IDH1-wildtype and IDH1-mutant genotype, silencing Chka or Cd274, blocking PD-L1 with an antibody, and reading the consequences by RT-qPCR, RNA sequencing, flow cytometry of surface PD-L1 and high-resolution 1H NMR of dual-phase cell extracts. The two genes proved reciprocal in both genotypes: silencing either transcript raised the other, and silencing choline kinase roughly doubled PD-L1 at the cell surface. Antibody blockade did something the silencing did not. In IDH1-wildtype cells it lowered soluble phosphocholine, the only one of twenty-two aqueous signals to survive correction for multiple testing, and raised total lipid per cell without changing lipid composition, whereas silencing PD-L1 raised phosphocholine instead; in IDH1-mutant cells neither change occurred. The transcriptome drew the same boundary, engaging a sterol programme and lowering glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in wild-type cells only. The interferon response did not respect that boundary and rose under every perturbation in both genotypes. Removing PD-L1 from inside the cell and blocking it from outside are therefore not the same intervention, and the metabolic half of the response stops at the IDH1 genotype.

papers.title: Single-agent PD-L1 blockade and tumour volume in orthotopic GL261 glioma, with an exploratory lipid analysis of the treated tumours
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has not yet changed outcomes in glioblastoma (GBM), and in immunocompetent mouse glioma the effect of a single blocking antibody is usually reported as survival rather than as tumour volume with its own confidence interval. We treated mice bearing orthotopic GL261 gliomas with anti-PD-L1 as a single agent in an IDH1-wild-type and in an IDH1-mutant line, and followed tumour volume by MRI. At day 14, tumours of treated animals were 0.33 times the volume of control tumours in the IDH1-wild-type line (95 % CI 0.21 to 0.53; p < 0.001; 16 anti-PD-L1 and 20 control animals) and 0.42 times in the IDH1-mutant line (0.22 to 0.78; p = 0.006; 10 and 10 animals), from a linear mixed model of log tumour volume over days 8 to 16. Diffusion imaging of the same tumours gave a higher apparent diffusion coefficient in the treated IDH1-wild-type tumours, by 23 % over the whole tumour (p = 0.027), and lower fractional anisotropy in the treated IDH1-mutant tumours, by 25 % over the whole tumour (p = 0.023), and in the periphery of the IDH1-wild-type ones, by 24 % (p = 0.005). We also imaged the lipid composition of treated and control IDH1-wild-type tumours ex vivo by mass spectrometry imaging: relative to the healthy brain of the same section, sphingomyelin was higher in the treated tumours and phosphatidylcholine species shifted towards shorter chains (p = 0.016 for both). In orthotopic GL261 glioma, anti-PD-L1 as a single agent reduces tumour volume in the IDH1-wild-type and in the IDH1-mutant line.

papers.title: FN1 is produced by cancer-associated fibroblasts and carries no immune-exclusion signal beyond the collagen program: a two-cohort single-cell re-examination in non-small cell lung cancer
papers.abstract: Fibronectin 1 (FN1) has been proposed as a macrophage-derived driver of T-cell exclusion and AP-1-mediated resistance to checkpoint blockade in lung cancer. The human evidence was never tested against the two confounders most likely to generate them: collagen/extracellular-matrix (ECM) abundance and dissociation-induced immediate-early gene (IEG) expression. We reanalyzed two public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cohorts, GSE148071 (42 treatment-naive tumors) and GSE207422 (15 specimens; 92,330 cells), with 24 pre-treatment bulk transcriptomes. Malignant epithelium was called by compartment-level inferCNV; FN1 source was attributed within macrophage and fibroblast compartments and by ligand-receptor scoring; exclusion associations were tested by partial Spearman correlation with permutation testing, controlling for a 22-gene collagen/ECM signature; AP-1 regulon activity was quantified before and after masking the 27-gene IEG panel, benchmarked against a dissociation-stress score. FN1 was produced predominantly by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs): the FN1-positive fraction was higher in CAFs than macrophages in both cohorts (paired Wilcoxon P = 1.6 x 10?? and P = 0.002), and CAF-to-epithelium communication exceeded macrophage-to-epithelium by about six-fold (median 0.32 vs 0.05, P = 1.5 x 10??). An independent lung-adenocarcinoma cohort (GSE131907) replicated this cell of origin (FN1-positive fraction 0.88 in CAFs versus 0.44 in TAMs; 11 paired samples, P = 0.001). The bulk FN1-cytotoxic association ({rho} = -0.53, P = 0.008) disappeared after collagen adjustment across three independent FN1 scoring schemes (partial {rho} = +0.21 to -0.16, all P > 0.33) and was not reproduced at single-cell level. Sample-level AP-1 activity tracked dissociation stress ({rho} = 0.88, P = 2.3 x 10??); IEG masking shrank histology-associated effect sizes by 40-64%, yet masked activity remained stress-coupled ({rho} = 0.82). FN1 is therefore a CAF product whose apparent link to immune exclusion is absorbed by the collagen program, and AP-1 readouts from dissociated tissue are stress-dominated; stress scores should accompany AP-1-based resistance claims.

papers.title: Multimodal Virtual Screening Identifies Candidate Inhibitors of Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells Across Breast Cancer Subtypes
papers.abstract: Polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) are associated with treatment resistance and tumor recurrence yet identifying compounds that selectively suppress these cells remains challenging. Here, we developed a multimodal machine-learning framework to prioritize PGCC-suppressing compounds by integrating chemical fingerprints, drug-induced cellular morphology, transcriptomic perturbation profiles, and biologically informed molecular annotations. Using screening data from four breast cancer cell lines, we systematically evaluated feature selection, drug representations, and ensemble learning strategies. PGCC-guided feature selection reduced morphology dimensionality by 93.7% while identifying cell-cycle-enriched gene sets, linking predictive features to biologically relevant processes. An ensemble integrating complementary predictors achieved a mean Pearson correlation of 0.403 and an enrichment factor of 5.46 among the top 5% of ranked compounds. In held-out screening data, the ensemble recovered 27.9% of experimentally identified hits, representing approximately 5.6-fold and 2.5-fold improvements over random selection and the best individual predictor, respectively. We subsequently prioritized 21,367 compounds from an external library for experimental evaluation. Experimental testing identified six candidates that preferentially suppressed PGCCs in at least three paclitaxel-treated cell lines. Notably, AZD-8055 and voxtalisib reduced PGCC abundance by at least 70% across all four cell lines. These results establish a multimodal computational-experimental strategy for phenotype-directed drug discovery and provide new candidates for targeting treatment-induced PGCCs.

papers.title: A machine learning framework for evolutionary model classification
papers.abstract: Machine learning algorithms are increasingly used across scientific disciplines, but remain absent from several areas of comparative biology. One example is evolutionary model selection, which typically relies on likelihood-based methods to identify the model among a candidate set that best explains trait evolution across a phylogeny. This approach requires all candidate models to have a tractable likelihood function yet this may not the case for complex models. Alternative likelihood-free inference methods are available but their application is limited in scalability and flexibility. Both classes of methods struggle with discriminating models that yield statistically similar patterns in trait data. Here, I introduce a machine learning framework to perform evolutionary model classification from comparative data. Using simulated datasets, I demonstrate that the approach improves model discriminability relative to conventional likelihood-based model fitting but does not overcome model non-identifiability. I then revisit an analysis of early burst signals in comparative data to assess how a machine learning approach alters the patterns of early burst support obtained through likelihood-based inference. Finally, I discuss future extensions of this framework and their potential to improve both our representation and understanding of evolutionary process-to-pattern mapping.

papers.title: Temporal genomic erosion estimates require demographic and technical validation
papers.abstract: Genetic diversity is a fundamental component of biodiversity, and temporal genomics offers a powerful approach to monitoring genomic erosion and informing conservation assessments. However, robust inference of genetic diversity loss requires consistency with demographic expectations and careful evaluation of technical biases between historical and modern sequencing data. Here, we combine population-genetic simulations, independent reanalyses of temporal genomic datasets, comparisons of alternative heterozygosity estimators and controlled experiments of historical-like DNA degradation to evaluate the reliability of genomic erosion estimates. Using data from four bird species included in a recent study reporting average diversity losses of 43-49% across 62 species (Liu et al., 2026), we show that losses of this magnitude generally require severe, sustained population bottlenecks accompanied by extensive runs of homozygosity (ROH), which were uncommon in the modern genomes examined. Heterozygosity estimates were highly sensitive to analytical methods: ANGSD recovered substantial declines (23-42%), whereas HEARTY and ATLAS showed little or no loss (-1% to +9%). Experimentally introducing historical-like DNA degradation into reads from genetically identical individuals generated apparent declines of up to 42% with ANGSD, demonstrating that sequencing artefacts alone can produce signals comparable to those reported. We further evaluated estimator performance using the Chatham Island black robin, which experienced a documented severe demographic collapse. HEARTY and ATLAS recovered substantial heterozygosity losses (56-59%), although additional degradation experiments revealed dataset-specific biases in both methods. Together, our findings demonstrate that technical artefacts can mimic or obscure genuine genomic erosion, with effects varying across datasets and analytical approaches. Integrating demographic expectations, complementary genomic indicators and explicit assessments of sequencing biases is essential for reliable use of temporal genomics in biodiversity monitoring and conservation assessments.

papers.title: Shifting roles of incomplete lineage sorting and gene flow across the diversification of Old World deer
papers.abstract: Rapid radiations often generate pervasive phylogenetic discordance through incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) and gene flow, making evolutionary relationships difficult to resolve. Old World deer (subfamily Cervinae) exemplify this process, in which morphological convergence and cytonuclear discordance have long complicated intergeneric relationships and reticulate histories. Here, we analyzed whole-genome resequencing data from 10 individuals representing 10 species across all six extant Cervinae genera. Integrating phylogenomic reconstruction, molecular dating, and genome-wide discordance and allele-sharing tests, we investigated the roles of ILS and introgression. Our nuclear species tree shows that Axis porcinus and Dama dama diverged sequentially at the base of Cervinae (at 7.69 Ma and 6.56 Ma, respectively), followed by the split between Cervus and the Elaphurus-Rusa-Rucervus clade at 5.29 Ma, and rapid diversification within Cervus during the Early Pleistocene (2.23 - 1.01 Ma). Discordance patterns shifted across timescales: Miocene divergences were primarily associated with ancestral ILS, whereas Pliocene and Pleistocene divergences showed stronger signatures of gene flow. These included ancient introgression between Elaphurus davidianus and ancestral Cervus, as well as recent hybridization between Cervus albirostris and Cervus canadensis. Around the Miocene-Pliocene transition (~5.3 - 5 Ma), warmer, wetter conditions promoted woodland recovery, followed by Pleistocene climatic oscillations. These environmental changes likely reshaped habitat connectivity, facilitating secondary contact and gene flow among diverged lineages, particularly during recent radiations. Together, these findings highlight the roles of ancestral polymorphism and episodic gene flow in shaping the reticulate evolutionary history of Cervinae.

papers.title: H2O: Improving Detection in Large-Scale Gene Family Expansions and Associated Phylogenomic Inferences
papers.abstract: Ancient whole-genome duplications (WGDs) have shaped flowering plant evolution, but their placement is sometimes uncertain, especially in clades primarily studied through transcriptomes. In such datasets, peaks in synonymous substitutions among paralogs (Ks) and phylogenomic gene-duplication mapping can identify large-scale gene family expansions (GFEs), but these approaches may disagree and, on their own, cannot distinguish WGD from chromosomal duplication or other genome-scale duplication mechanisms. These discrepancies may stem from biological processes such as diploidization, hybridization, and incomplete lineage sorting, or from systematic biases introduced by hidden gene paralogy that current pipelines fail to address. Here, we present H2O (homolog-to-ortholog), a workflow that integrates Ks distributions with tree-based conservative gene duplication calls (node-partitioned Ks distributions) and orthology inference with duplication-informed data-filtering methods. It improves the detection and placement of transcriptome-inferred GFEs while reducing errors from hidden paralogy. We evaluated H2O using simulated datasets and three empirical datasets (Ericales and two Caryophyllales subclades), refining large-scale GFE placements and comparing phylogenomic outcomes with those of ASTRAL-Pro and Yang and Smith (2014). Across empirical datasets, node-partitioned Ks distributions improved confidence in large-scale GFE placement and, under conservative phylogenetic data filtering, significantly reduced associated gene tree discordance. Reduced discordance comes at the cost of substantial data removal. Through simulation, we demonstrated that H2O's data-filtering methods effectively removed all paralogous relationships that orthology inference methods sometimes report, reducing gene tree discordance. These results highlight the need to treat transcriptome-inferred GFEs cautiously, integrate multiple lines of evidence, and explicitly account for hidden paralogy in plant phylogenomics.

papers.title: Studying evolutionary dynamics across the entire Sequence Read Archive
papers.abstract: Querying the Sequence Read Archive traditionally relied on submitter metadata that is often missing, inconsistent, or wrong. Logan changed that picture by assembling the archive for direct sequence searches with kmindex and LexicMap. Yet hits are not alignments. Variation and uneven coverage fragment genes across assembly pieces, while redundant outbreak isolates overwhelm comparative evolutionary tools. We built disassembler to reconstruct complete coding sequences from unitig graphs or contigs, thin clonal duplicates, and build deep cohorts spanning up to millions of runs. From 4.99 million SARS-CoV-2 hits, disassembler recovered 910,848 strict and 1,153,319 permissive Spike sequences. Paired with the Aeon tools (HyphAeon, RhizAeon, and ChronAeon), downsampled cohorts ([≤] 200 haplotypes) resolve evolutionary dynamics in seconds without iterative tree search. Across SARS-CoV-2, microbiome obelisks, and Helicobacter pylori, panels recover a 2.55-fold Omicron clock acceleration, gyrA drug-pocket rigidity, oipA/vacA/Spike co-selection, 57.4% mixed obelisk infections with six mosaic tracts, and 5.37-fold vacA recombination enrichment.

papers.title: Come together: Coordinate deconvolution of viral recombination, reassortment, and epistatic survival
papers.abstract: Viral subtyping and recombination detection underpin taxonomic curation, clinical resistance tracking, and real-time outbreak surveillance. Community nomenclature systems--such as HIV-1 circulating recombinant forms (CRFs), SARS-CoV-2 Pango lineages, and Influenza A genotype catalogs--have created indispensable shared vocabularies, yet rapid archive growth and frequent cross-lineage chimerism now invite a complementary layer that unites speed, provenance, and statistical rigor across viral families. Here, we present EGGMAN (Exact Genomic Genealogy and Mosaic Ancestry Nomenclature), a unified framework that separates mapping physical parental coordinates against a principled, non-mosaic founder basis (Tier 1) from statistically guarded assignment to established epidemic clones (Tier 2). By combining reference-free recombination scrubbing (RhizAeon), emergence-anchored founder rooting (ChronAeon), and portable pathogen specifications, one engine processes contiguous genomes (HIV-1, SARS-CoV-2, wildlife sarbecoviruses) and segmented reassortants (Influenza A) at thousands of sequences per second on a laptop or in a browser--preserving legacy clade names while giving emerging chimeras transparent, coordinate-based identifiers on Day 1. Across public surveillance archives, EGGMAN harmonizes the HIV-1 reference catalog and genealogy, reconciles >120,000 clinical pol records in Stanford HIVDB, separates emerging CRFs and a monophyletic regional lineage from convergent recombination hotspots, and tracks unannotated H5Nx reassortants and SARS-CoV-2 X* waves without temporal lookahead. Finally, census-level mapping across 761 HIV-1 mosaic lineages reveals a two-stage selective sieve separating within-host protein-folding viability (gp120 and Gag-CA cores) from between-host preservation of an intact 3' regulatory and envelope cassette.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Cycles of Evolution: Specific Dissipation, Ecological Recovery, and Evolutionary Memory
papers.abstract: In the post-extinction period, does evolutionary capacity recover together with biomass? We address this question with a consumer resource model in which strategies lie on a rate-yield (opportunist gleaner) trade-off and dissipate the substrate free energy they do not conserve in biomass. We track biomass-specific dissipation, s, a model-based proxy for specific entropy production. After a reset, abundant resources favor fast, low-yield strategies, and s is high; this rate selection resembles, but does not demonstrate, the maximum power principle. As resources are drawn down, competitive exclusion favors high-yield strategies and lowers s, provided that turnover is low and that affinity is lost faster than growth rate is gained along the trade-off. In finite populations, the high-dissipation phase returned after a reset only if a reservoir of costly strategies, here dormant propagules, had persisted since those strategies were last abundant; its return fell from 199 to 33 of 200 runs as the reservoir decayed. Biomass recovered in every run, and sooner when the high-dissipation phase failed to return. Ecological recovery and recovery of evolutionary capacity are therefore distinct. We state falsifiable predictions for calorimetric chemostat experiments with graded bottlenecks and controlled resting-stage survival.

papers.title: A TRAIL-R4 splice isoform sensitizes cancer cells to TRAIL-induced apoptosis
papers.abstract: The immune system can recognize and eliminate tumor cells through the secretion of specific cytokines, including TRAIL (tumor necrosis factor-related apoptosis-inducing ligand). TRAIL triggers apoptosis by binding to its death receptors, TRAIL-R1 and TRAIL-R2. However, cancer cells can evade TRAIL-mediated cell death through the expression of decoy receptors, TRAIL-R3 and TRAIL-R4, which can bind TRAIL but lack the ability to initiate apoptotic signaling. Here, we focused on the decoy receptor TRAIL-R4, also known as TNFRSF10D, and investigated an alternative splicing event that generates a transcript lacking exon 3. This exon-skipping event results in a truncated receptor isoform, termed iTRAIL-R4, which lacks part of the ligand-binding domain. Structural biology analyses confirmed that TRAIL cannot efficiently bind to iTRAIL-R4. Interestingly, whereas the canonical TRAIL-R4 isoform protects cancer cells against TRAIL-induced apoptosis, overexpression of iTRAIL-R4 sensitizes cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated cell death. Furthermore, combining iTRAIL-R4 expression with different therapeutic treatments enhances the sensitivity of cancer cells. Collectively, our findings highlight the potential of iTRAIL-R4 to help counteract therapeutic cancer resistance and recurrence. They further support the therapeutic relevance of modulating TRAIL-R4 alternative splicing to shift cancer cells toward a more apoptosis-sensitive state.

papers.title: Testing the impact of gut microbiome rewilding on the health of captive bumble bees
papers.abstract: Animals and plants are often raised in captivity for food, companionship, conservation, or research purposes, a practice which typically reduces the diversity of their microbiomes. This loss of microbial diversity may in turn compromise host nutrition, pathogen resistance, and reproduction. Microbiome "rewilding"--restoring microbes present in the wild, but lost in captivity--has been proposed as a way to ameliorate these effects. However, it has only been tested in a handful of taxa. We evaluated the efficacy of microbiome rewilding in bumble bees (Bombus), a group of ecologically and agriculturally important pollinators. In captivity, bumble bees retain host-specialized "core" gut bacteria, but lack the diverse environmental bacteria commonly present in the gut of wild bees. We inoculated captive B. impatiens colonies with five species of environmental bacteria isolated from wild B. impatiens. Rewilding did not affect bee survival, reproduction, or nutrition (glycogen or lipid levels). We conducted a second experiment with Arsenophonus, the environmental bacterium exhibiting the highest colonization rate in captive bees, to test its role in resistance against an opportunistic bacterial pathogen. While inoculation with gut material from captive bees (which is dominated by core bacteria) completely protected hosts from pathogen infection, Arsenophonus inoculation had no effect. These findings demonstrate that microbiome rewilding is not always effective for sustaining the health of captive hosts.

papers.title: Role-Aware Line-Graph Neural Networks for Interpretable Prediction of Pairwise Microbial Interactions
papers.abstract: Predicting how microbial species affect each other's growth is a key challenge in microbial ecology. Using one of the largest available pairwise interaction datasets, comprising 20 soil bacteria co-cultured under 39 carbon conditions (15{,}074 directional measurements), we predicted whether one species has a positive or negative effect on the growth of another from monoculture growth, metabolic profiles, and phylogeny. Existing machine learning approaches treat each measurement as an independent sample, although experiments that share a species under the same condition are biologically related. We therefore represented the data as a role-aware line graph: each node is one directional measurement, and two nodes are connected when, under the same carbon condition, they share the same effector or the same affected species. This allows graph neural networks (GNNs) to pass information between related interactions. Our role-aware GAT-SAGE model achieved an F1-score of 81.38% for one-way prediction, outperforming the 73.79% previously reported for Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). For two-way interaction types (mutualism, competition, and parasitism), GAT-SAGE reached a macro F1-score of 60.34%. This exceeded the 55.71% of a neural network without graph structure but was below the 64.24% of XGBoost. Mutualism remained difficult to predict for all models. Layer-wise relevance propagation showed that one-way effects depend mainly on monoculture growth, whereas two-way interaction types depend more on the carbon environment. Encoding the dependency structure of interaction experiments thus adds information beyond the features of each measurement and provides interpretable insight into microbial interactions.

papers.title: Identification of three apicoplast transporters with crucial roles in the malaria parasite life cycle
papers.abstract: Malaria parasites depend on an intriguing endosymbiotic organelle, the apicoplast, for survival throughout the life cycle. The apicoplast is enclosed by four membranes and transport of metabolites across these membranes remains poorly understood. Thus far, only twelve (putative) membrane transport proteins have been confirmed to localize to the organelle. We report a crucial function in the apicoplast of three previously uncharacterized members of the major facilitator superfamily of transporters in Plasmodium falciparum. MCP1 and UMF are essential for asexual blood-stage parasites and could only be deleted in the presence of an alternative pathway for producing isopentenyl pyrophosphate. Deletion of either gene resulted in disruption of apicoplast morphology and loss of the organellar genome, suggesting that both are required for apicoplast housekeeping. In contrast, MCP2 was dispensable in the blood stages yet essential for parasite development in the mosquito. Oocysts in the mosquito midgut lacking MCP2 were significantly smaller than wild-type oocysts and produced no sporozoites, similar to when apicoplast fatty acid metabolism is disrupted. Differences in apicoplast morphology became apparent five days after infection, with MCP2-deficient oocyst apicoplasts displaying a less extended, sometimes fragmented, network with thinner branches. Taken together, we identified three novel apicoplast transporters, with MCP1 and UMF being essential for asexual blood-stage development by supporting apicoplast housekeeping, and MCP2 being crucial for parasite growth in mosquitoes, possibly by facilitating fatty acid metabolism.

papers.title: Skeletal Growth Retardation in Diamond Blackfan Anemia Syndrome Arises From Cell-Autonomous, p53-Dependent Mesenchymal Progenitor Defects Independent of Hematopoietic Failure
papers.abstract: Ribosomopathies are a class of disorders caused by defects in the structure or function of the ribosome and are characterized by tissue-specific abnormalities. Diamond Blackfan anemia syndrome (DBAS) features skeletal anomalies in addition to anemia, but whether these reflect primary mesenchymal dysfunction remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that skeletal growth retardation in DBAS is cell-autonomous, arising from RPS19 haploinsufficiency in mesenchymal progenitors without leading to hematopoietic failure. RPS19 haploinsufficient mice exhibit shorter limbs due to growth plate disorganization. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals impaired chondrocyte differentiation, with decreased Runx2 expression and activation of the p53 pathway across the chondrocyte trajectory. Surprisingly, in vivo translation remains unchanged, arguing against a translational collapse and implying the p53-dependent nucleolar surveillance as main mechanism of growth defect. Accordingly, Trp53 deletion in RPS19 haploinsufficient mice rescues all skeletal defects in a dose-dependent manner. Importantly, RPL5 haploinsufficiency in mesenchymal progenitors does not result in skeletal defects, establishing ribosomal protein gene specific functions in the mesenchyme. These findings demonstrate that nucleolar surveillance functions as a developmental checkpoint controlling growth plate formation, with direct implications for understanding the tissue-specific manifestations of ribosomopathies.

papers.title: The blue dragon nudibranch (Glaucus atlanticus) shifts to less venomous prey in the Mediterranean, with no evidence of defensive microbial symbionts
papers.abstract: Glaucus atlanticus ("blue dragon"), is an aeolid nudibranch that acquires chemical defense through sequestration of nematocysts from its primary prey, the highly venomous Physalia physalis ("Portuguese man-of-war"). In August 2025 hundreds of G. atlanticus individuals appeared near Alicante (Spain), prompting temporary beach closures due to concerns about potential envenomation. This unusual occurrence, in a region where P. physalis is typically absent, raises questions about the trophic ecology and defensive strategies of this species under novel environmental conditions. Here, we used COI metabarcoding of gut to characterize the diet of G. atlanticus and combined it with 16S rRNA gene sequencing of cerata, gut, mucus, and central dorsal epidermis to assess potential microbial transfer from alternative prey that could contribute to the synthesis of defensive compounds, given that the role of microbes in chemical defense of aeolid nudibranchs was not assessed previously. We detected a trophic shift toward alternative cnidarian prey, including Pelagia noctiluca and Porpita porpita, which are not considered highly hazardous. Microbiome comparisons with P. porpita, as well as comparison of core microbiomes across different body parts of G. atlanticus, revealed no evidence of prey-derived transfer of mutualistic bacteria. Instead, G. atlanticus harbored distinct microbial communities dominated by environmentally widespread taxa, including potential opportunistic pathogens, with no indication of symbionts associated with defensive functions. Altogether, these findings indicate that, despite trophic flexibility, G. atlanticus may have limited capacity to maintain its defensive mechanisms in the absence of its primary prey.

papers.title: Bulk RNA-seq data of an Adherent-Invasive Escherichia coli Strain ZVL and Its exuR-Knockout Mutant
papers.abstract: Adherent-invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) is a subtype of pathogenic E. coli associated with Crohn's disease. AIEC strains are characterized by the ability to adhere to and invade epithelial cells, survive and replicate within macrophages. Despite many years of research, the mechanisms of virulence and pathogenicity still remain not fully understood. Previous studies have shown that the virulence-associated phenotype of some isolates can be reversibly eliminated by changing the growth medium, specifically by switching from M9 minimal medium supplemented with propionate to M9 supplemented with glucose. This phenomenon was also observed in ZVL, an AIEC isolate from our laboratory collection. Since certain sugar acids, particularly hexuronates, have been shown to contribute to gut colonization by other bacterial pathogens, their role in AIEC has not been reported in the literature. Therefore, we aimed to investigate whether the hexuronate degradation pathway influences the adhesion and invasion properties of AIEC. To this end, we generated a CRISPR-based deletion mutant lacking exuR, which encodes a transcriptional repressor of the Ashwell pathway, and performed bulk RNA sequencing of wild-type ZVL and the exuR mutant. Both strains were grown in M9 minimal medium supplemented with either glucose or sodium propionate. Caco-2 cell assays were used to assess bacterial adhesion and invasion under both growth conditions. Our results suggest that deletion of exuR affects the invasion phenotype following growth in propionate-supplemented medium.
